point.outcome: Train one picking finger to move while the other fingers stay quiet enough to block on purpose.

practice.title: One digit moves
practice.tempo: No metronome at first; then 50–60 BPM
steps: Pick one note with the thumb.
Return the blocking finger to its string without lifting the other fingers.
Repeat with index and middle as separate motions.
Play the four-note sequence only after all three motions feel small.
hearSeeFeel: Hear a clean stop with no extra string ringing.
See the non-picking fingers remain nearly still.
Feel no squeeze in the wrist or thumb joint.
practice.success: Five repetitions sound alike and the resting fingers do not travel with the active finger.
practice.easier: Mute the strings with the bar hand and practice only the right-hand motion.
practice.challenge: Move the same four-note pattern to a neighboring string group without making the motion larger.

diagnostics.response: Freeze two fingers on their strings and let only the active digit complete one pick-and-return cycle.

diagnostics.problem: The block makes a loud clank
diagnostics.response: Reduce the return distance and land on the string instead of striking through it.
Keep your normal musical approach. Use this drill to learn the pick-blocking motion as an additional choice.

guides.title: What Are the Pedals Really Doing?

claims.text: Pedal changes are taught as interval functions, with licks as musical results.
Major, minor, dominant-seven, and major-seven formulas are checked against deterministic interval rules.
The listen-name-play sequence is companion practice guidance.

setup.copedent: Standard 10-string E9; A and B pedals, E raises/lowers
requirements: Know the open E major grip
Be able to engage one pedal at a time
prerequisites: Basic scale-degree numbers are helpful, not required

point.outcome: Hear pedals as changes to interval roles instead of memorizing them only as lick controls.

sessions.instruction: Hold a small grip and identify how each pedal changes the harmony.

practice.title: Say the interval before the lick
practice.tempo: Free time; let each pitch settle
steps: Play the open string without a pedal.
Name its role in the E chord.
Engage only the assigned pedal or lever and name the new role.
Play the two-note change inside a grip and describe the chord color it creates.
hearSeeFeel: Hear the destination pitch before pressing the control.
See which strings change and which remain anchors.
Feel the pedal stop without adding bar pressure.
practice.success: You can predict the interval change before you hear it on three different strings.
practice.easier: Work only with the A pedal: fifth to sixth.
practice.challenge: Describe one familiar lick entirely as interval changes.

diagnostics.problem: I remember the pedal but not what it changes
diagnostics.response: Use one string at a time and say the before/after interval out loud before playing.
Anchor every number to an audible open-E note, then move the same relationship to another key.

diagnostics.problem: A lever produces a chord name I do not recognize
diagnostics.response: List the sounding intervals first; name the chord only after the notes are accounted for.

practice.title: Home → neighbor → home
steps: Play the home-position chord and name its function.
Choose one chord tone or scale tone one or two frets away.
Move to it without changing the chord context in your head.
Return to a stable chord tone, then build a route in the other direction.
hearSeeFeel: Hear the home chord continuing underneath the connecting note.
See a destination before moving the bar.
Feel the bar arrive squarely instead of searching after the attack.
practice.success: You can leave and return to the position in both directions without losing the chord sound.
practice.easier: Use only one string and one neighboring fret.
practice.challenge: Connect the same two positions with a different string group or pedal state.

diagnostics.problem: I can copy the lick but cannot find another route
diagnostics.response: Name the destination interval, then search for that same role on a nearby string before adding chromatic notes.

diagnostics.problem: Major 7 and dominant 7 are blurring together
diagnostics.response: Check the seventh: natural 7 for major 7, flat 7 for dominant 7. Keep the concepts separate before locating grips.

diagnostics.problem: I lose track of which pedal state I am in
diagnostics.response: Pause at every destination and say pedals up, A, B, A+B, or lever name before continuing.
